claims.text: Above 900 K, the friction spike and loss of wear resistance are caused by a transition from thermally activated dislocation annihilation to localized shear-induced amorphization.
Suppression of stacking-fault energy contributes to the proposed transition.
The alloy cannot sustain a stable dislocation network under the imposed high strain rate.
The coating and Cu matrix begin as perfect single crystals without pre-existing defects.
The intervention consists of nanoindentation to 30 Å at 10 m/s and at 300, 600, 900, and 1200 K.
A shear-induced amorphous zone forms at the indenter-coating interface.
Stacking-fault collapse and thermally activated dislocation annihilation mediate formation of the amorphous zone.
The amorphous zone causes a loss of load-bearing crystalline structure.
Above 900 K, thermal energy exceeds the activation barrier for dislocation climb and cross-slip.
Activated climb and cross-slip cause rapid dislocation annihilation or mechanical annealing.
Reduced stacking-fault energy promotes partial-dislocation formation, followed by rapid merging or annihilation that prevents work hardening.
Loss of shear strength under the high indentation strain rate triggers a localized transition to an amorphous state.
Adhesive bonding of the amorphous layer causes the friction spike and catastrophic loss of wear resistance.
The friction coefficient decreases from 300 K to 600 K because of increased dislocation mobility.
The friction coefficient spikes at 900 K and 1200 K.
Wear resistance drops precipitously above 900 K.
HCP-like atom counts transiently increase before the amorphous transition.
Dislocation line length in the contact zone falls to near zero at 1200 K.
At 300 K and 600 K, deformation is dominated by dislocation nucleation, glide, and multiplication, while the coating retains crystalline integrity.
At 600 K, thermal annealing reduces dislocation density.

contradictions.description: The mechanism identifies reduced stacking-fault energy as a driver of amorphization and the friction spike, but the falsification rule says that eliminating the spike by stabilizing stacking-fault energy would falsify that driver. Elimination of the spike under that intervention would instead support the proposed causal role.

The causal transition is repeatedly stated to occur above 900 K, whereas the predicted friction spike explicitly includes 900 K. The inclusion or exclusion of the 900 K condition at the onset is therefore inconsistent.
